tldr: We propose SCOPE, a method that distills diffusion score curvature (Hessian) to estimate control-ready analytical uncertainty tubes in under a millisecond, completely bypassing expensive Monte Carlo sampling.
hero_caption: Top: SCOPE leverages score curvature to turn trajectory forecasts into control-ready Gaussian tubes in real time. Bottom: The estimated uncertainty integrates into robot control both as a policy prior that adapts MPPI exploration covariance and as a world model that predicts future occupancy of other agents (humans).
overview:
Diffusion models have rapidly become popular in robotics planning and pedestrian forecasting as powerful generative models capable of capturing complex, multimodal trajectory distributions. However, using the model's predictive uncertainty—its probabilistic spread—in real-time control faces a major hurdle. Extracting explicit uncertainty from standard diffusion models requires Monte Carlo sampling across dozens of reverse diffusion iterations. This process is too computationally heavy to fit into the cycle times required for closed-loop control.

To tackle this, the authors focused on a key insight: local uncertainty (the precision matrix) is already directly embedded within the geometric curvature of a trained score model (the Hessian of the log density). Drawing from the Laplace approximation, a steep drop in likelihood around a nominal trajectory implies high confidence (a thin tube), whereas a flat drop reflects large uncertainty (a thick tube). The proposed approach, SCOPE, distills this score curvature into a lightweight neural network during training using Hessian-vector products (HVPs). At inference time, a single forward pass combined with a structured block-banded plus low-rank solver outputs a Gaussian tube with per-timestep covariances in under 1 ms.

In experiments, SCOPE matched the uncertainty quality (measured by NLL) of heavily sampled ensemble methods in pedestrian trajectory forecasting at a fraction of the computational cost. Furthermore, integrating SCOPE into MPPI (sampling-based MPC) demonstrated superior closed-loop performance across maze navigation, crowd avoidance in busy intersections, and real-world pick-and-place inside a shelf using a Franka Panda arm, benefiting both adaptive exploration and collision risk assessment.
contributions: Proposed SCOPE, a lightweight module that extracts control-ready, per-timestep uncertainty from diffusion models in under 1 ms without extra sampling.
Structured the trajectory precision matrix as block-banded plus low-rank, enabling efficient HVP training and linear-time marginal covariance queries during control.

Integrated SCOPE uncertainty tubes into both world models (collision risk assessment) and policy priors (adaptive MPPI exploration covariance), demonstrating improved closed-loop performance across diverse tasks including real-world manipulation.

sections.heading: Why extract diffusion uncertainty for real-time control?
sections.summary: Capturing predictive uncertainty from diffusion models is essential for collision risk assessment in robot control, but conventional Monte Carlo sampling is too slow. This paper proposes SCOPE, which distills score curvature to produce control-ready uncertainty tubes in a single forward pass.
sections.details:
Diffusion models are widely used as control policies (motion generation) and world models (forecasting environments and other agents) thanks to their ability to represent high-dimensional, multimodal distributions. However, in interactive robotics settings where robots share space and collaborate with humans, predicting a single most likely trajectory is not enough. Robots need to capture the aleatoric uncertainty inherent in future behaviors. They must know not just where an agent is likely to go, but also how wide the variation around that path is, in order to maintain proper safety margins.

The challenge is that diffusion models represent uncertainty implicitly within their generative process. The standard way to extract it is Monte Carlo sampling over dozens or hundreds of reverse diffusion rollouts. Even with GPU batching, the computational latency is too high for real-time closed-loop control loops. Reducing sample counts speeds things up, but at the cost of poor estimation accuracy.

Here is the key idea. The authors noted that the score function (the gradient of the log density) in a trained diffusion model already captures the local geometry of the trajectory space. Under the Laplace approximation, the negative Hessian (curvature) of the log density directly corresponds to the precision matrix (the inverse covariance). SCOPE distills this score curvature into a lightweight precision head during training. At inference, a single forward pass through the diffusion model plus the precision head instantly yields a Gaussian tube ready for direct use by a controller.

sections.heading: Basics of trajectory diffusion and MPPI control
sections.summary: We review the formulation of discrete-time diffusion models for trajectory generation and the fundamentals of MPPI, a sampling-based nonlinear optimal controller. Key takeaways: terminal score functions approximate the gradient of clean data log density, and MPPI performance heavily relies on its exploration covariance design.
sections.details:
Let's review the two foundation technologies behind this work.

The first is the diffusion model for trajectory forecasting. In contrast to the forward process that progressively adds noise to clean trajectories $\mathbf{y}_0$, a neural network learns a reverse denoising process. This is practically equivalent to learning score functions $s_\theta(\mathbf{y}, \mathsf{s}) = \nabla_\mathbf{y} \log p_\mathsf{s}(\mathbf{y})$, which represent the gradient of the log density at each noise level. In particular, at the terminal step ($\mathsf{s}=0$), the score $s_\theta(\mathbf{y}, 0)$ approximates the clean data log-density gradient $\nabla_\mathbf{y} \log p(\mathbf{y})$, and its curvature holds the key to uncertainty extraction.

The second is Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control. MPPI is a sampling-based control algorithm capable of handling nonlinear dynamics. It adds Gaussian perturbations $\delta\mathbf{u}_t \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{\Sigma}^\mathbf{u})$ to nominal control sequences, rolls them out through the dynamics, and performs importance-weighted updates based on rollout costs. While MPPI gracefully handles non-differentiable costs, relying on a fixed exploration noise covariance $\mathbf{\Sigma}^\mathbf{u}$ poses a major challenge: the controller easily gets trapped in local minima in narrow or concave obstacle-dense environments.

sections.heading: Fast tube estimation via score curvature distillation and structured precision
sections.summary: SCOPE extracts uncertainty from the local Hessian of the score function around representative trajectories from a multimodal backbone. Using a block-banded plus low-rank structure and HVP-based training, it delivers Gaussian tubes directly pluggable into MPPI with minimal online overhead.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Control Interface: Mixture of Gaussian Tubes
SCOPE outputs a mixture of Gaussian tubes, each defined by a representative trajectory $\boldsymbol{\mu}_k(\mathbf{c})$ as its centerline and a structured precision matrix $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_k(\mathbf{c})$ capturing local spread. The mode probabilities $\pi_k$ represent discrete global intents, while the tube width (marginal blocks of the inverse precision matrix) represents local uncertainty within each intent.

### 3.2 Multimodal Diffusion Backbone
Drawing many samples from standard diffusion models and clustering them in post-processing is too slow for real-time control. Instead, the authors use a backbone conditioned on discrete latent variables $z \in \{1, \dots, K\}$. This cleanly separates qualitatively distinct future modes (e.g., turning left vs. right) and directly produces per-mode probabilities and nominal trajectories.

### 3.3 Training and Structuring the Score-Curvature Precision Head
Score curvature reflects uncertainty because, according to the Laplace approximation, the negative Hessian $-\nabla_\mathbf{y}^2 \log p(\mathbf{y})$ near a density peak corresponds directly to the Gaussian precision matrix $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^*$. However, computing a dense Hessian online in high-dimensional trajectory space is prohibitive. The authors introduce two solutions:

- Block-banded plus low-rank structure: Trajectories exhibit Markov properties, meaning temporal coupling is dominated by adjacent timesteps (block-banded matrix $\mathbf{L}\mathbf{L}^\top$), while long-range correlations can be captured via a low-rank term $\mathbf{R}\mathbf{R}^\top$. This structure allows linear-time marginal covariance queries at each step using fast Cholesky decomposition and the Woodbury matrix identity.
- Distillation via HVPs and Hutchinson's method: Rather than instantiating the full target Hessian, the network computes Hessian-vector products (HVPs) along random probe vectors $\mathbf{u}$ via automatic differentiation during training to supervise the precision head $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_\phi$. Heavy second-order computations remain confined to offline pre-training.

### 3.4 Integration into Downstream Control
The estimated tubes serve two control roles. When used as a world model to forecast surrounding agents, the robot computes an upper bound on collision probability (chance constraints) from the time-varying Gaussian mixture and penalizes the MPPI cost function accordingly. When used as a policy prior for the robot itself, MPPI adapts its exploration noise covariance $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_t^\mathbf{u}$ to match the tube covariance. This enables smart exploration: wider search in open spaces and tighter, collision-free sampling in narrow passages.

sections.heading: Validation across prediction accuracy, inference speed, and closed-loop control
sections.summary: We evaluated SCOPE on a pedestrian forecasting benchmark, Maze2D navigation, crowd intersection navigation, and real-world Franka shelf pick-and-place. SCOPE matched or exceeded ensemble uncertainty quality in under 1 ms, significantly boosting closed-loop control success rates.
sections.details:
The experiments address three questions: Q1 on uncertainty quality and runtime, Q2 on policy exploration efficiency, and Q3 on world-model collision avoidance.

### 4.1 Basic Characteristics of the SCOPE Precision Head
Uncertainty quality was evaluated using Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL) in a pedestrian Y-junction setting. Baselines included a Linear Kalman Filter (LKF) and MID-Ensemble, which fits Gaussian mixtures over 64 to 256 diffusion samples. SCOPE matched or outperformed ensemble baselines in NLL, even under dense crowd conditions. In terms of runtime, while ensembles slowed down by up to $7\times$ with increasing sample counts, SCOPE computed and calibrated precision matrices in under 1 ms on an A5000 GPU. Structurally, the full block-banded plus low-rank formulation achieved better NLL than block-banded-only or diagonal variants.

### 4.2 Case Study 1: Maze2D Navigation
SCOPE was evaluated as an MPPI policy prior in a non-convex 2D maze. Standard Diff-MPPI with fixed covariance struggles: wide exploration causes many rollouts to hit walls, resulting in dangerous trajectories that graze obstacles, while narrow exploration gets stuck in local minima. Diff-MPPI + SCOPE adaptively widens exploration at openings and contracts it in narrow passages, achieving the highest success rates and shortest path lengths across all rollout budgets.

### 4.3 Case Study 2: Y-junction Crowd Navigation
An autonomous mobile robot navigates a crowded intersection with 3 to 12 pedestrians. While diffusion-based methods outperformed No-Forecast (NF) and LKF, sampling-based MID-Ensemble suffered from high latency that degraded control frequency and capped success rates. SCOPE evaluated chance constraints accurately in real time without sacrificing loop rates, achieving clearly superior success rates in dense settings with 9 and 12 pedestrians.

### 4.4 Case Study 3: Real-World Franka Arm Manipulation
A 7-DoF Franka Emika arm performed a non-convex, confined pick-and-place task, retrieving a tomato from inside a shelf and placing it on an upper rack (30 trials per condition).
- Static environment: Diff-MPPI with fixed exploration chose a tight side-entry path, becoming trapped by joint limits or colliding with obstacles and causing timeouts (TO). SCOPE chose a flexible frontal entry mode and adapted its search, achieving the highest success rate and lowest collision rate.
- Dynamic environment: A human hand reached into the shelf area. Without forecasting, the robot reacted too late and collided with the shelf. The ensemble baseline (64 samples) maintained control frequency but lacked accuracy, while 128 samples introduced update lag. SCOPE detected future hand occupancy early, retreated smoothly, and achieved the highest overall success rate.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Turning diffusion uncertainty into a robotic asset
sections.summary: We proposed SCOPE, which instantly extracts control-ready Gaussian tubes from diffusion models via score-curvature distillation. It substantially enhances closed-loop performance across forecasting, navigation, and real-robot manipulation while preserving real-time execution.
sections.details:
This work introduced SCOPE, a lightweight module that adds control-ready uncertainty to diffusion trajectory models. By distilling local score-curvature information via Hessian-vector products during offline training and leveraging a block-banded plus low-rank structure at inference, SCOPE achieves sub-millisecond covariance computation without repeated sampling.

This enables real-time evaluation of pedestrian chance constraints and adaptive MPPI exploration covariance tuning, leading to superior closed-loop performance in maze navigation, crowd avoidance, and real-robot shelf manipulation. SCOPE marks a practical step forward in bringing the expressive power of diffusion models into safety-critical robot control.

sections.heading: Assumptions and future challenges
sections.summary: Key limitations include reliance on diffusion backbone quality and an assumption of low-dimensional state inputs. Extending SCOPE to out-of-distribution scenarios and raw observations like images or point clouds represents important future work.
sections.details:
Because SCOPE distills uncertainty directly from score curvature, it fundamentally depends on the diffusion backbone being properly trained. In regions with poor training data coverage or where the backbone fails to separate modes cleanly, the predicted uncertainty tubes may become over- or under-confident, undermining calibration.

Additionally, current evaluations rely on relatively low-dimensional geometric state inputs, such as robot and pedestrian coordinates. Extending the framework to extract control-ready uncertainty tubes directly and end-to-end from high-dimensional raw observations, such as camera images and point clouds, remains a crucial direction for real-world deployment.

sections.heading: Markovian analysis and theoretical grounding of the precision matrix
sections.summary: The appendix details diagnostic validations of the Laplace expansion that justify local Gaussian approximations, alongside theoretical motivations for the block-banded sparse structure based on temporal trajectory independence.
sections.details:
The appendix provides mathematical justifications and diagnostic experiments supporting the proposed method.

### Validation of the Laplace Approximation
To verify whether nominal trajectories decoded from the diffusion model lie near local modes, score curvature was analyzed across 3,000 anchor trajectories in the Y-junction environment. Remarkably, 94.8% of the resulting matrices were positive definite, and the median root-mean-square position residual between the curvature center and the decoded trajectory was just 1.33 cm. This confirms that a second-order Taylor expansion around nominal paths provides a highly valid local Gaussian approximation.

### Markov Sparsity in the Precision Matrix
The block-banded structure finds its theoretical basis in Gaussian Graphical Models. In discrete-time dynamical systems governed by $b$-th order Markov properties, states separated by more than $b$ steps become conditionally independent given intermediate states. Since zero entries in a Gaussian precision matrix correspond directly to conditional independence, off-diagonal blocks beyond bandwidth $b$ naturally vanish. Visualizing the ground-truth teacher precision matrix confirms that near-diagonal banded components dominate, justifying the combination with a low-rank term to capture residual global constraints (such as goals and obstacles).

captions.F5: Structure visualization of the teacher precision matrix. Linear scale plots (left, center-right) reveal strong diagonal dominance, while symmetric log scale plots (center-left, right) clearly highlight the Markovian near-diagonal banded structure alongside low-rank global patterns.

takeaways: Score gradients (curvature) in diffusion models directly capture local precision matrices (inverse covariance), completely bypassing expensive Monte Carlo sampling.
Restricting trajectory precision matrices to a block-banded plus low-rank structure leverages physical Markov properties to allow linear-time marginal covariance queries.
Extracted uncertainty serves not only as a world model for obstacle collision risk, but also as an effective guide to dynamically widen or narrow MPPI controller exploration noise.
limitations: Relies on the training quality of the underlying diffusion backbone; poor data coverage or distorted scores can degrade uncertainty calibration.
Evaluations are currently limited to low-dimensional geometric state spaces (e.g., positions), leaving end-to-end integration with raw sensor data like images or point clouds as future work.
